question_html: Accounting Standard 19, Lease is applicable on following Leases:

options.A: Lease agreements to explore for or use of natural resources, such as oil, gas, timber metals and other mineral rights.
options.B: Legal owner of an asset conveys to another party in return for a payment or series of periodic payments, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time.
options.C: licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — AS 19 defines a lease as the conveyance, by the legal owner of an asset, of the right to use that asset to another party for an agreed period in return for a payment or series of payments; this is the definition itself. Options (A), (C) and (D) are all activities/agreements AS 19 explicitly excludes from its scope (natural-resource exploration/use rights, licensing agreements for films/patents/copyrights, and land lease agreements).
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Definition of a lease versus AS 19's explicit scope exclusions

question_html: A Machinery was given on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is ₹3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000 units, Year III 40,000 units, Year IV 65,000 units, Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. This is an operating lease (the machine returns to the dealer after the 3-year term, with 2 years of economic life remaining). Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000, recovered progressively in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output is consumed during each period of use — not amortised flat over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output

question_html: As per Accounting Standards, difference between the Gross Investment and the present value of Minimum Lease Payments under finance lease (from the standpoint of the lessor) and Unguaranteed Residual Value accruing to the lessor is recorded as
answer_html: Answer: (A) Unearned finance income — per AS 19, this exact difference (Gross Investment less the sum of the present value of MLP and the present value of unguaranteed residual value, both at the interest rate implicit in the lease) is the lessor's unearned finance income, recognised over the lease term on a pattern reflecting a constant periodic rate of return on the net investment.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.8): Lessor's gross investment less net investment equals unearned finance income

question_html: Sargam Ltd. (the lessee) has taken machinery on lease from Dhun Ltd. (the lessor) for 13 years on annual lease payment of ₹50,000. The life of the machine is 15 years. How this lease arrangement should be classified and why:

options.A: Operating lease because lease payments are being made annually and the value of asset is not available.
options.B: Finance Lease because lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred.
options.C: Operating Lease because it is not stated that the asset will transferred to lessee at the end of lease term.
options.D: Finance Lease because the leased asset is of a specialized nature such that only the lessee can use it without major modifications being made.

answer_html: Answer: (ii) — AS 19 lists "the lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred" as one of the situations that would normally lead to a lease being classified as a finance lease. Here the lease term (13 years) is 13/15 ≈ 87% of the machine's 15-year economic life, clearly the major part, so this is the correct classification and reasoning; options (A) and (C) reach the wrong conclusion (operating lease), and (D) reaches the right conclusion for the wrong reason (specialised-nature indicator is not supported by any fact given in the question).
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Finance lease indicator - lease term for the major part of the asset's economic life

question_html: X Ltd. sold Plant & Machinery having WDV of ₹ 60 lakhs to Y Ltd. for ₹ 75 lakhs (Fair value of ₹ 75 Lakhs) and the same plant was leased back by Y Ltd. to X Ltd. The lease back is in the nature of operating lease. The treatment will be:

options.A: X Ltd. should amortize the profit of ₹ 15 lakhs over the lease term.
options.B: X Ltd. should recognize the Profit of ₹ 15 lakhs immediately.
options.C: No profit/loss, as fair value is equal to sale price.
options.D: Y Ltd. should recognize the profit of ₹ 15 lakhs immediately.

topic_text: AS 19 — Leases (5.10): Sale and leaseback - leaseback as operating lease, sale price equal to fair value

question_html: As per AS 19, unearned finance income is:

options.A:
the difference between (a) the gross investment in the lease and (b) the present value of
      minimum lease payments under a finance lease from the standpoint of the lessor; and any unguaranteed
      residual value accruing to the lessor, at the interest rate implicit in the lease.
options.B:
the payments over the lease term that the lessee is, or can be required, to make excluding
      contingent rent, costs for services and taxes to be paid by and reimbursed to the lessor.
options.C:
the aggregate of the minimum lease payments under a finance lease from the standpoint of
      the lessor and any unguaranteed residual value accruing to the lessor.
options.D: the lease is the gross investment in the lease less unearned finance income.

answer_html: Answer: (A) — this is AS 19's own definition of unearned finance income. Option B actually defines "minimum lease payments," option C defines "gross investment in the lease," and option D describes "net investment in the lease" (gross investment less unearned finance income), not unearned finance income itself.
topic_text: AS 19 — Leases (5.3): Definition of unearned finance income

question_html: X Ltd. sold Plant & Machinery having WDV of ₹60 lakhs to Y Ltd. for ₹75 lakhs (Fair value of ₹75 Lakhs) and the same plant was leased back by Y Ltd. to X Ltd. The lease back is in the nature of operating lease. The treatment will be:

options.A: X Ltd. should amortize the profit of ₹15 lakhs over the lease term.
options.B: X Ltd. should recognize the Profit of ₹15 lakhs immediately.
options.C: No profit/loss, as fair value is equal to sale price.
options.D: Y Ltd. should recognize the profit of ₹15 lakhs immediately.

answer_html: Answer: (B) X Ltd. (the seller-lessee) should recognise the profit of ₹15 lakhs (₹75 lakhs sale price − ₹60 lakhs WDV) immediately. Under AS 19's sale-and-leaseback rules for an operating lease-back, when the sale price is equal to the fair value of the asset, the transaction is treated as a normal sale and any resulting profit or loss is recognised immediately by the seller-lessee, with no deferral over the lease term (deferral applies only to a finance lease-back, or to specific fair-value-mismatch cases under an operating lease-back).
topic_text: AS 19 (5.10): Sale and leaseback as an operating lease where sale price equals fair value - profit recognised immediately by the seller-lessee

question_html: A Machinery was given on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is Rs. 3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is as follows: Year I 50,000 units; Year II 60,000 units; Year III 40,000 units; Year IV 65,000 units; Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000 — as a dealer/manufacturer lessor, the fair value (normal selling price) built into the lease is cost plus the stated profit margin: ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. The 3-year lease covers only part of the machine's 5-year economic life, so only the portion of that value corresponding to the output actually consumed during the lease term is recoverable through rent: output in Years 1-3 (50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units) is exactly half of the machine's total 5-year output (50,000+60,000+40,000+65,000+85,000 = 3,00,000 units). Value to be recovered over the 3-year lease = 50% × ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000, and equal annual rentals = ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.8): Manufacturer/dealer lessor selling profit; lease rental recovery apportioned by output consumed during a lease term shorter than total economic life

question_html: A dealer in machinery, Shakti Equipments Pvt. Ltd., leased out one of its machines to Delta Tools Ltd. on a 3-year operating lease, with equal annual lease rentals intended to yield a 20% profit margin on the cost of the machinery (₹3,00,000). Economic life of the machinery is 5 years; total expected output over its useful life: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000, Year III 40,000, Year IV 65,000, Year V 85,000. Delta Tools will use the machine for Years I–III only, then return it. Compute the annual lease rent that provides the dealer a 20% profit margin on cost.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. Since this is an operating lease, the dealer recovers this target progressively, in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output/value is consumed during each period of use — not by amortising the full amount over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the 3-year lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals over the 3 years: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output

The lessor has guaranteed a residual value of ₹20,000. However, lessor estimates that it would have a value of ₹5,000 only after 3 years. At what value the machinery would be recognised.
topic_text: AS 19 — Leases (5.8): Finance lease - lessee's initial recognition at lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments
